title: Growing money moves it forward in time
lead: Keep Meridian’s $1,000, 6%, one-year example.
prompt: The $1,060 includes the original $1,000 and $60 interest.

title: Which starting amount earned $60?
lead: Now the interest is known. The starting principal is missing.
prompt: We divided the interest earned, not the total ending balance.

title: Discounting brings the total back to today
lead: Now the known amount is the $1,060 future receipt.
prompt: Recovering principal from interest and discounting a total are different questions.

title: Build the interest and ending balance
lead: Open Simple interest. Inputs: C17 = $1,000; C18 = 6%; C19 = 1 year.
prompt: Build with cell references. What is included in the ending balance?

title: Check the forward calculation
lead: Compare your formulas before changing anything.
prompt: Interest is only the addition. Future value is the whole balance.

title: Bring the same money back to its start
lead: Use the same inputs and your completed C20:C21.
prompt: Build both formulas. Predict whether the two answers should agree.

title: Two routes recover the same $1,000
lead: Each formula reverses a different relationship.
prompt: Both return C17 because they use the same simple-interest model, rate, and time.

title: Checkpoint B: what must Meridian repay?
lead: Meridian borrows $18,500 for 8 months at 6.2% annual simple interest.
prompt: Predict: will repayment exceed $18,500? Explain your result in B31:G33.

title: Debrief B: separate interest from principal
lead: Eight months is 8/12 of a year.
prompt: The repayment returns $18,500 principal and adds $764.67 interest.

title: A day-based note uses the same logic
lead: Meridian’s note: $32,000 principal, 4.5% annual rate, 80 exact-interest days.
prompt: Build B6 on Note example. Then transfer the method to checkpoint A.

title: Checkpoint A: which year basis costs more?
lead: Same $42,000 principal, 4.8% annual rate, and 75 actual days.
prompt: Only the year basis changes. Predict first; explain the difference in B26:G28.

title: Debrief A: the smaller denominator matters
lead: The prefilled F7 and F9 links carry each year fraction into its interest calculation.
prompt: 75/360 is larger than 75/365. Use the basis stated in the agreement.

title: What earns interest in the second year?
lead: So far, only the original principal earns interest. What if earned interest stays invested?
prompt: Predict year 2 interest first. The prior $60 earns another $3.60 under compounding.

title: Choose the model before discounting
lead: Meridian will receive $1,120 after two years. Required annual return: 6%.
prompt: Both are valid under their stated assumptions. Our payment-stream challenge uses annual compounding.

title: Excel’s negative PV is a cash-flow direction
lead: Investor viewpoint: pay today; receive $1,120 at the end of year 2.
prompt: Use =-PV(C8,C9,0,C12) in C14 to show the positive magnitude for comparison.

title: Check by growing the payment forward
lead: Use the signed PV already calculated in C15.
prompt: A verification must use the same rate, time, and growth model.

title: Checkpoint C: what is the receipt worth today?
lead: Meridian expects $30,000 in 2 years. Use 6.5% annual compound discounting.
prompt: Explain the sign and the verification in B36:G38. Use the inputs in rows 16–18.

title: Debrief C: interpret both directions
lead: A payment today and a receipt later have opposite signs.
prompt: The negative PV is an outflow, not a negative investment value. The FV check recovers the receipt.

title: Extension: express a wait in annual periods
lead: Meridian expects $18,000 in 15 months at a 6% annual compound rate.
prompt: This example assumes fractional-period annual compound discounting. It is not simple interest.

title: Waiting longer lowers the value today
lead: Keep the future receipt at $100 and the annual compound rate at 6%.
prompt: Predict before comparing: why is the earliest receipt worth the most?

title: A higher required return lowers present value
lead: Keep the future receipt at $100 and the wait at three years.
prompt: Connect to the opening: what could make Meridian require a higher return?

title: Use both effects to predict the extremes
lead: Before calculating, identify the highest and lowest PV in the worksheet grid.
prompt: Highest: shortest wait + lowest rate. Lowest: longest wait + highest rate.

title: Diagnose the model before the challenge
lead: Same $18,000 receipt after two years; same 6% annual rate.
prompt: The challenge states annual compounding. Explain which denominator fits before building.

title: Bring one payment back before combining many
lead: Worked example: a separate $10,000 receipt at the end of year 2; 6% annual compound rate.
prompt: For several payments: discount each to today, then add their present values.

title: Challenge: which offer would you choose?
lead: Meridian can receive $75,000 today or the future payment stream below. Use 6% annual compounding.
prompt: Confirm E6. Build E12:E18; then recommend an offer in B19:E23 with one assumption that could change it.

title: Every payment must end at the same date
lead: Keep the annual discount rate fixed while each payment’s year changes.
prompt: Sum unrounded values: $84,602.28. E18 compares that total with E6.

title: Recommend using value today and assumptions
lead: Compare your evidence before revising your recommendation.
prompt: At the stated rate, Offer B has the higher PV. How could payment risk or a higher required return reverse that choice?

title: Defend the model, then defend the decision
lead: Return to our opening question: why can money today be worth more?
prompt: Opportunity cost, purchasing power, and payment risk inform the required return; do not add three percentages automatically.
